As you know better than anyone, Kosovo is a much smaller place than Bosnia, and one can cover more territory there in a relatively short amount of time than one could in a country that is several times larger.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But as a person who aspires to work as a scholar, although it doesn't sound right that someone who is about to turn 61 is about to get his PhD, that would really be a disgrace in the area where I come from, but perhaps it's different in your milieu, wouldn't it be professionally and morally unacceptable to study and research the crimes of one side in a post-war situation and not the other side in that war conflict? From a moral and professional point of view, can a scholar allow himself to do that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's interesting that you should bring that up, because actually my interest in the destruction of cultural property in the Balkans during the wars of the 1990s long predates my association with the Tribunal, and I have always been interested in all forms of cultural property. The difference in this case was that for the report that I submitted to the Tribunal, I had to adhere to the terms of the mission. However, as you point out yourself, if one is a scholar, one has a certain amount of intellectual curiosity and wants to see the whole picture, which is in fact what I tried to do even during my fieldwork. When I set out to do my fieldwork in Bosnia, one of the starting points, given that this fieldwork took place in 2002, already a number of years after the war, was to gather all information that was put out by various bodies, both secular and religious, about what had been destroyed during the war. Amongst that information, for my own purposes - it wasn't included in the report - I took great care to look at the information published by the Serbian Orthodox Church. They went through three editions of a book called: "Spiritual Genocide," "Duhovni Genocid," and I looked at that information. And when I was in the field, whenever it was possible to do so without making a great detour, I looked at the state of the Serbian Orthodox buildings about which claims of damage had been made. If you're interested, I can run down it very easily. It's 11 municipalities --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But I'm not interested. Please. You are using my time for nothing, in vain. I'm not interested in what you did. I'm interested in what your expert report contains. What you did, in terms of your own interest, that's your own private affair. You compiled a highly tendentious and one-sided expert report, and an uninformed observer could conclude that in this war, Serbs were war criminals who were systematically destroying Croatian and Muslim cultural monuments and religious buildings, on the one hand, and on the other hand there is no information to the effect that the same was done by Muslims and Croats; isn't that right? An objective, impartial person reading your expert report would have to come to that conclusion, that it's only Serbs who are criminals here, destroying churches and mosques?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you had let me finish my previous answer, I could have told you that in the 11 municipalities which I surveyed, there were a total of 14 Serbian Orthodox buildings, 13 churches plus one Episcopal palace, that had been either damaged or destroyed. Out of those 14 monuments, and that's the total, I visited nine of them and documented them for myself. In those same municipalities, you had 101 mosques and 27 Catholic churches that were damaged, and so that does allow one to draw certain conclusions. Unfortunately, I was not able to include this information in my report because that's not what I was asked to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You must know that many Serbian authors, not only Professor Slobodan Mileusnic, who dealt with this the most, but also Sasa Miric, Drago Jovanovic, Gordana Bundalo and Miloskova Darevic [phoen], then Milivoje Ivanisevic, and many others, made inventories and documented destroyed Serbian churches, cemeteries, parish homes, cultural monuments and so on, and the figure they reached was 700. Some of these were destroyed totally and some were damaged.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. According to the book "Duhovni Genocid," which is Professor Mileusnic's work, the total number he mentions for destroyed churches combined in Bosnia and Croatia is much less than that. I think it was 212. And we were talking -- when I mentioned 14, it referred specifically to the 11 indictments -- municipalities. There were areas in Bosnia where the Serbian cultural property suffered more than in others. Those were not included in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mention only the churches that were totally destroyed. However, according to the official information of the Serbian Orthodox Church, supplied to me by the OTP, and the number here is Y0039108, it says that it's only in five diocese in the territory of Croatia that 270 Serb religious facilities were destroyed. The OTP can find it under this number, because they're the ones who provided me with this document. So your information is not correct. You do like to turn things the other way around. If Professor Mileusnic says 270 destroyed, for you that's a total number, and on the other hand you make an inventory of destroyed/damaged buildings and you lump it all together. That's not right for a serious scholar. However, tell me, if you were tasked with submitting a report on destroyed cultural heritage, why did you not include all the buildings of cultural heritage, the real cultural monuments, rather, what is UNESCO-protected heritage or under state protection or local protection as an important local monument? You dealt with all sorts of monuments, Roman Catholic and Muslim, but not any Serbian ones, because not everything can be cultural heritage, not every church, not every mosque can be cultural heritage; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection. This is irrelevant. It goes to a tu quoque defence which the Chamber is well aware is improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the question you have just put to the witness, you have put it to him at least two or three times. It was a question I put to him right at the beginning. He answered the question. He explained to you why he prepared the report in the way he had. He addressed the destruction of the mosques and of the churches, because that is what the Prosecution had asked him to do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I was wondering how you're going to calculate the Prosecutor's time that he spends on putting the wrong kind of questions, and now you're lecturing me on what happened in the examination-in-chief. I have the right to raise all the questions that were dealt with in the examination-in-chief. I did not participate. The Prosecution did, the Judges did; I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, you're quite right. But just one thing. Put a question to him -- you're putting a question to him which he has answered already, and he's answering in the same way. You put your question three times, and he has answered the same way every time. I don't mind if he answers differently with regard to your question; fine. I don't have the feeling that the witness was going this way and that he would answer the questions differently. However, as far as relevance is concerned, you know as well as I do, Mr. Mundis, that tu quoque is not something which is acknowledged by this Tribunal, but if you would like to provide the context and say that it wasn't only Roman Catholic churches and Muslim mosques that were destroyed, when at some point the witness said he had prepared things for himself because he was particularly interested in this, you cut him short and told him that you weren't interested. So I'm trying to understand what point you're trying to make.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as soon as you and your colleagues of the Trial Chamber establish that this Prosecution expert got things confused and was given the task of dealing with the destruction of cultural heritage in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then he turned it the other way around, he turned it into a report on the destruction of Islamic and Roman Catholic buildings, I thought that at that moment you would send him out of the courtroom and reject his report, but you didn't do that. If cultural heritage -- the destruction of cultural heritage was his task, then he had to deal with the entire cultural heritage of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Serbian Orthodox cultural heritage there is hundreds of years older than Islamic heritage there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please answer this question. The title of your paper is: "Destruction of Cultural Heritage in Bosnia-Herzegovina." On the basis of this title, one could believe that the Orthodox churches would be part of this paper, but it seems that you restricted your survey to the mosques and the Roman Catholic churches. Can you explain this to us, Witness? Well, you're an expert, I know. Normally speaking, in my country, and in your country it must be the same - in this Tribunal it's somewhat more complicated - when one of the parties asks to have an expert report, then a letter is sent. The party sends this letter, and the assignment is clearly spelled out. Unfortunately, in your report, your assignment has not been mentioned. There is no document in support of this. When you testified before the ICJ at the request of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the litigation between Serbia and Montenegro and Bosnia-Herzegovina, I assume that someone must have sent you a letter, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina sent you a letter, saying that they wished you to testify as an expert to discuss such-and-such a point. What I'm interested in is this, because I've put the question to you already and you've answered already, but Mr. Seselj is not satisfied with your answer: What exactly were you asked to do as part of your expert survey? Was it to study destruction on a massive scale or were you to focus only on the Croatian churches and on the mosques?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, first of all, at the peril of pointing out the obvious, the title of my report is not limited to the title proper. It is also subtitled, which gives the limitations of its scope, both in terms of geography and time its limitation to non-Serb cultural heritage. As for the terms of my assignment, they are described in detail in my expert report, in the introduction, starting from paragraph 7, going through paragraph 11; that is, on pages 0469-3672, 73 and 74. I unfortunately did not include the letter I did receive from the Office of the Prosecutor in each of these cases, asking me to do it, but I summarised the contents, and I'm sure that the OTP can unearth from its files the corresponding documents setting the terms of my mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand, sir, but I'm not levelling any criticism at you. But I'm putting myself in the shoes of someone who goes on the internet and follows these proceedings and say, "Well, there's an expert in the courtroom. He's been asked to report on the destruction of cultural heritage in Bosnia-Herzegovina." This is what the person sees. The person doesn't see the subtitle, which is written in small print. And the person listens and says, "Well, there are only churches and mosques that were destroyed," and therefore infers that nothing happened to Orthodox churches. You see, this is what the issue is all about. The title should have been: "Destruction of Cultural Heritage in Bosnia-Herzegovina," i.e., the mosques and the Roman Catholic churches. Like that, everything would have been quite clear, what the field of your survey was. But this is your title, which is -- and you explain that in paragraph 7, you explain what you have been asked to do. But in paragraph 7, you mention the Milosevic trial. We have not been seized of this matter, so this complicates the issue even further. Well, you have answered some of the questions. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor, and please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, in 1995 you testified before the US Congress, before the Congress Committee on Security and Cooperation in Europe; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And on that occasion, you testified about the destruction of the Muslim and Roman Catholic religious buildings in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I pose the question to you: Why did I not receive transcripts of this testimony by Mr. Riedlmayer before the US Congress from the Prosecution, although the Prosecution was aware of that? I cannot contact the Prosecution directly. I can only contact the Prosecution via the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, now, the expert purportedly testified before the US Congress on the same topic, and Mr. Seselj is saying why was he not given his testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're checking our records right now. Of course, the first question in any such inquiry is whether it's in our possession. If we don't have it, then we don't have it to disclose. Certainly, Congressional testimony is in the public domain and could be found by anyone who was looking for it. But I am checking our records right now to see if, in fact, we do have the transcripts of that testimony and, if we do have it, whether or not it was disclosed. So perhaps if we move on, I'll be in a position to address that issue a little bit later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, I assume that as an historian, following the political developments in the Balkans, the war, and in particular the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, have often encountered the political activities of the Serbian Radical Party and my political statements, speeches and so on, I am not a nobody to you. I'm not somebody of whom you had heard for the first time when you were given the task; is that so? I assume that it is so.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have heard of you, and I very well remember, during my fieldwork in Bosnia in 2002, there was a gentleman on the street who was handing out the glossy magazine of the Bosnian branch of your party, and in the back it included advertisements for your books. I can't say that I have read all of them, but I have read some of the things that you've written.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber wouldn't be able to read everything even if they did nothing but read until the rest of -- for the rest of their lives, not because I have a low opinion of their abilities but because of the huge volume of my writings. But I would like to know something. Have you ever heard of me or any other official of the Serbian Radical Party advocating the destruction of Muslim or Roman Catholic religious buildings, of us inciting or justifying such destruction? Have you ever heard anything of the sort?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not my assignment, to look for that kind of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that, first of all, a priest of the Serb Orthodox Church, Patriarch Pavle, has on several occasions made public calls against the destruction of the religious buildings belonging to other faiths; Muslim, Roman Catholics and so on? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the president of the Republika Srpska, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, issued an order in 1993 to the effect that the police are ordered to strictly protect all the religious buildings in the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of that particular order. In fact, in cross-examination in the Milosevic case, he produced that very order, and I read it in court. It was also stated in court at that time, however, that after that order was issued, the destruction continued unabated. And, for example, in 1993, in Banja Luka, 13 more mosques were destroyed after that order was issued, in a town that saw no fighting, which was under curfew at night and which was fully under the control of Dr. Karadzic's police and military. And so I don't know what actual effect such an order had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, that's the gist of it. The effectiveness of an order, if, on the one hand, you never heard of any Serb political or religious official advocating the destruction of religious buildings belonging to other fates, and if it in fact happened in practice, it means that their authority was not strong enough to prevent it. Is that the only -- is that not the only logical conclusion we can draw, or that there are hypocrites who publicly order the prevention of the destruction and at the same time secretly condones and advocates such destruction, but it is simply unthinkable that something like that would happen? Do you agree with what I'm saying, but please be very brief in your answer, because I want us to go on to address the very essence of the case.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gladly. I think it's entirely possible for people to say one thing in public and to do something quite contrary to that behind the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, do you have any evidence for any particular case in which somebody said something about churches and mosques in public and then did the opposite behind the scenes; is there any evidence?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just mentioned the fact that after that order signed by Radovan Karadzic was issued, I believe it was May of 1993, the destruction of mosques and Catholic churches continued unabated right to the end of the war. I can, if you like, cite specifics.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But as an historian, I am aware of this destruction. You don't have to point that out to me. I am aware that Orthodox, Roman Catholic churches and Muslim mosques were destroyed. This is not controversial. There was a detail that was controversial, as far as I was concerned, in your report that had to do with manipulating photographs. But as an historian, you have to know that in 1993 there was an attempted coup, military coup against Radovan Karadzic in Banja Luka itself. Banja Luka itself was blocked. It no longer obeyed the central authorities in Pale. I don't know if you recall this coup, attempted coup. It was in September of 1993.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a vague recall of it, yes. But as I recall, he then managed to regain control of Banja Luka, and the destruction of mosques happened before the coup and after the coup. And by the end of 1993, there was not a single mosque left standing in Banja Luka out of 16 before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When you embarked on this task, as a scientist, as a scholar, you had to put in place certain systematisation. Your methodology had to be based on certain rules. So in the systemisation, or typology, you had to make a clear distinction between the religious buildings that are on the frontlines that could have been destroyed in the combat activities launched by one or other side, and religious buildings that were destroyed not in any kind of fighting deep behind the frontlines; that would be the basic methodological distinction to be drawn in your task?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you've read my report, you will see that I addressed this from several aspects. First of all, looking at context, which I addressed in some detail a little while ago, were buildings around the churches or mosques destroyed to the same degree that the churches or mosques were. That gives you some idea. Secondly, I did look at the context in terms of whether there was fighting going on at the time of destruction, and there are many places, such as Nevesinje, Banja Luka, Bosanski Samac, Bijeljina, where the destruction happened after the Serb authorities had full control of the situation. For example, in Bijeljina, the main destruction happened in the spring of 1993, which was almost the year after there had been no fighting in Bijeljina. So, yes, it's addressed in some in detail in my report. And it's also clear from my report that the only buildings that escaped damage, to a large degree, meaning that were only lightly damaged, were buildings that were either on the frontlines and far enough behind the frontlines so they weren't badly hit, or a limited number of cases of buildings which hadn't been officially registered as active mosques or churches which were in Serb-held territory but for some reason did not make it onto the list of things to be gotten rid of. It's the only way I can explain a situation like in Zvornik, where you had an inaccessible mosque on a cliff top in Kuslat being destroyed, whereas a mosque that was only a few feet from the highway was untouched, and my contention is that this says something about the spontaneous versus planned nature of the destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As an historian, for instance, when you came to Nevesinje, you ascertained that the mosques in Nevesinje had all been destroyed, despite the fact that there was no fighting there. You had to have learned the basic facts as to when it happened, who was in power in the municipality at the time and who might be responsible. Had you done that, you would have learned that at that time the municipality was governed by Vuk Draskovic's party, the Serb Restoration Movement. That is one of the two municipalities in Republika Srpska ruled by the Serbian Restoration Movement. The other one was Sipovo up there in Bosnia. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not my responsibility to establish which particular party may have been responsible for the destruction. My focus was on documenting the destruction and, to the extent possible, establishing when it occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let's be clear. You are right to say this. I don't contest it. There were two things. You're an expert. You go on-site, you make pictures. You're capable -- you don't need to make deep studies to make a difference between a Catholic church or an Orthodox church or a mosque. Therefore, you could have, first of all, had a series of photographs before the conflict and then after the conflict, and draw conclusions, so many mosques, so many churches were destroyed, seriously or not at all. But when one looks at your report, one sees that you have interrogated some people to help you, and this is understandable. These persons gave you some information, some hearsay information, which you put in your own report. Why not? That's what you've done. I have nothing to say against that. But coming back to the example given by Mr. Seselj for Nevesinje as a place where there were no fights, but mosques were destroyed, and there I start wondering why you did not go to the town hall or the municipality building to ask where -- or perhaps at the police station, to ask how is it possible that in a place where there was no fight, mosques have been completely razed to the ground? Why didn't you do this so that some people might have told you, yes, the municipality is held by X or Y, it's a complicated matter? This may seem a bit strange, odd. You have an answer in particular in places where there was no fighting, so if there was no fighting in those places, a simple mind could see two possible causes; either people who came from elsewhere in the framework of a programmed operation with a big means, because as you told us, there were explosives used, and that could be one cause, or a second cause, the people of the municipality themselves may have decided to raze the mosque to the ground, or the Catholic Church. So why for some do you gather information about this or that specific element and in other places you don't do anything about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my purpose in getting any kind of statements revolved around the issue of when something was destroyed. If, in the process of me asking that question, the informant provided other information, I put it down. But as you note yourself, I am not someone who is empowered to depose people, to collect sworn statements or anything of the sort, and that certainly was not my assignment for this mission. My mission was to document the destruction and to find out when it happened. I tried to make sure that the buildings I saw destroyed hadn't been destroyed before or after the war, and if they were destroyed during the war, I tried, to the best of my ability, to cross-check any information provided to me from multiple independent sources. Of course, these were not always available, but when they are, I list them in my entry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While you were speaking, I had a look out of curiosity on paragraph 52 of your report. You note this monastery, this Franciscan monastery with 60.000 books destroyed, and now I see you speak of Serb troops, and then you describe this. This is very strange, very odd. Here, we've got a lot of details, and in other cases none. So did you actually -- were you aware of that, is it possible that in certain cases you were aware of things you could have done and which you didn't do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My mission mentioned not only places of worship but also archives and libraries, and the only way I could get information on archives and libraries was by, as in this case, consulting the librarian of the institution. I would think that he would be in the best position to provide firsthand information on what was in the library and what he knew about its destruction. This was the kind of approach that I could only take under special circumstances such as this. In other -- but I treated it much like I treated other cases. I didn't just take his word for it. I looked up all published information on the incident and on the library, and I included that in my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, when you were given the assignment from the Prosecutor to compile an expert report within the frameworks of the legal proceedings against me, the trial against me, did you at that time have any prejudices against me? Did you consider that I was some infamous leader of paramilitaries, somebody engaged in ethnic cleansing and things like that? Did you consider me anything like that, did you have that view of me, that prejudice against me?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. Frankly, the political aspects of it are not of great interest to me. My specialty is what this report addresses, and I would figure that, you know, other people would have the job of assessing whatever political aspects there were. I'm not a political scientist, and generally speaking, as a historian, I like to look at things which are far enough back in time that the dust has settled. So as far as you personally are concerned, I reserve judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I very much appreciate the fact that you presented views about me in such an honest way and that you reserve judgement and had no prejudices, but we come to a key point here where I'm catching you out in lies, Mr. Riedlmayer. May we have document number 1 placed on the overhead projector, please. You say you did not consider that I was the leader of notorious paramilitary organisations and someone who is engaged in ethnic cleansing, whereas I have a text of yours here dated the 22nd of December, 2004. It is your text on crimes in Brisevo, in Prijedor Municipality. Do you remember that article of yours? And look at the portion I've marked. And this is what you say here. You say that in a destroyed Roman Catholic church, my name was written up in Cyrillic, it said "Seselj," and then you said I was the leader of the Serbian Radical Party and of its notorious paramilitary organisation or militia now awaiting trial in The Hague. That's what you wrote at the time, whereas you say that you had no prejudice against me. So here we have your opinions of me before you received your project and assignment, and then -- just a moment, please, just wait. Towards the end of the text, you go on to say, it is line 5 from the bottom, that the Bosnian Serb Army and Seselj's paramilitaries cleansed at enormous human cost this place Brisevo. That's what you wrote, is it not? That's your text; right? Just "yes" or "no," please.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not say "yes" or "no." I would simply say that the first part, that you're the head of the Radical Party and that the Radical Party has a paramilitary organisation, is simply a statement of fact. It's not prejudicial. The last part there about the cleansing of Brisevo, at that point there had been already testimony about what happened at Brisevo, and, you know, I did include the fact that Brisevo was cleansed by paramilitaries. But I would also note that this is an informal e-mail message I sent to someone, and someone posted it on the web site. It's not something that is a sworn statement or part of my report. And as you, yourself, points out -- point out, this occurred before I was commissioned for my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, precisely the problem is there, there is the problem. Witness, before you were asked to draft your report, which I remind you that the expert is unbiased, you draft a text, 22 December 2004, in which, without adding too many niceties, you say the paramilitaries -- you mention the paramilitaries of Mr. Seselj, the cleaning of Brisevo, and anybody who reads this text can see that the person responsible is Mr. Seselj, and that is -- in fact, you add, "awaiting trial in The Hague," so you indicate there is a case -- a lawsuit in The Hague, and after that you accept to become an expert. Can't you see any problem in this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sir, I would -- Your Honour, I would urge you to look at my report, where I do not assign any responsibility to either Mr. Seselj or to his followers. The report is unbiased in terms of it deals with facts, presents those facts to the best of my ability to do so accurately, and draws conclusions which emerge from the facts and not from any preconceived notion. The fact is that in terms of what I did for the report, I think there is nothing in there that can be challenged as prejudicial on its face. You know, consider the function that I was performing when I did the report versus this particular item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the text of 2004, what allows you to say that Seselj's paramilitaries cleansed or cleaned -- what did you base yourself to reach such conclusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Various materials. Again, this is not a formal conclusion, it's an informal text, but it also emerges from having read reports on what happened in Brisevo. Again, it's not a legal document in the sense that I footnoted anything or, you know, put in elaborate sources. What suggested to me to include that phrase is the information in reports on the destruction of Brisevo and the fact that there were graffiti inside the destroyed church. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, now that I've caught you out in a lie, I'm going to provide you with a piece of information first and then ask you your opinion about it. The Brisevo case was dealt with in the judgement of Radoslav Brdjanin, the first-instance judgement, in paragraphs 411 and 412. I hope that the Registry can find that and have it up on our screens. I have the translation into Serbian, but may we have paragraphs 411 and 412, where the Brisevo case is described, and no mention is made of the Serbian Radical Party at all or Seselj's men either, not a single word about any of that. So why do you think that is? Paragraph 411 and 412 of the judgement.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please refresh my memory. When was the Brdjanin judgement issued?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, four or five years ago, as far as I remember. I'm not quite sure of the exact date. Let's say that it was about four years ago. Well, the OTP must know that. No, it's the 1st of September, 2004. It says there. That's the judgement. It's the judgement of the Chamber -- Trial Chamber of 2004, and the paragraphs are 411 and 412. Have you got that, Judges? And you can see that no mention is made there of either Seselj's men or the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the Registrar promised that we would see 411 and 412 on the screen, so we're just waiting for that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that going to be outside my time available, if we're waiting, or shall I carry on while you're waiting for that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, let's proceed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: While you were in Brisevo, you took four photographs, do you remember that, and you published them on the internet? One photograph shows the whole church. The second one is from a distance, where you can see the destroyed roof of the church, and a closer-up image of the destroyed church. And the last photograph is inside the perimeter of the church. Can we place that on the overhead projector? And nowhere is this graffiti where it says "Seselj." Why didn't you take a photograph of that? That would have been a good thing to see. You see that the lighting inside the church was fine. It had no roof, so that meant that the lighting is fine. So if you take the roof off a house, you get very good light, so why didn't you do that? Is that your photograph?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not my photograph. That particular photograph is from the Sivko Merica's [phoen] book, and you can see him in the church there. I do have photographs of the interior of the church and I do have a photograph of the graffiti, but I did not post them on the web site. In fact, I didn't post this web site at all. I sent information to someone at Haverford College, who then posted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I see. Very well, Mr. Riedlmayer. Did you write at one time that the Serb nationalists in Republika Srpska enacted some racial laws against the mixing of genes, according to which every non-Serb who would marry a Serb woman or who had sexual relations with her would be deemed to have committed a crime?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember writing that based on published information in 1993. As you can see, that particular item is dated, I believe, the summer of 1993. The war was still going on, and there were reports coming in that, for example, non-Serbs were made to fly white flags on their houses, to wear special armbands, and this was among the things that was being reported in the press at the time. This was while the war was still in progress. At that point, I think Biljana Plavsic had yet to make her famous statement about the degenerate genes of Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's leave Biljana Plavsic alone. She's a collaborator of The Hague Tribunal, as she did work for them, and dirty work for the Western powers in Republika Srpska. But let's look at this text, and it is document number 3. First of all, let's see the title page so that we can see the heading. It's a brief history of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then turn to page 3 straight away, page 3. And here you speak of the persecution of Muslims, Croats and even Gypsies and Jews in Banja Luka and other occupied Bosnian towns. So who occupied those Bosnian towns, I ask you, Mr. Riedlmayer?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb Army occupied them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did the Serbs occupy themselves, then? In Banja Luka, they were a considerable majority in town and in the surrounding villages. Did they occupy themselves, the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the Serb nationalist parties in Banja Luka took power by a coup on the eve of the war in Banja Luka, which is why Banja Luka saw no fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, didn't a coup take place in Sarajevo, when the Muslims and the Croats, in a one-sided manner, in spite of Serb opposition, proclaimed unilaterally the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Do you realise that without the Serb people, no one had the right to declare independence for Bosnia-Herzegovina? As a historian, you should know that the Serbs were a constituent people of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is taking us outside of the topic here, but I can answer if you like. To the best of my understanding, what happened in 1992 was a vote by the Bosnian parliament, and the Bosnian parliament declared independence. And this independence was then recognised by foreign countries, and Bosnia was admitted into the United Nations. I'm not a constitutional scholar. I cannot tell you whether or not this was in accordance with the constitution of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you find out later that there were no Serb laws against the mixing of genes and that it was never proclaimed that every Serb who would have had sex with a non-Serb woman or married a non-Serb woman was not a crime? Did you realise that later?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know now that certain things have been substantiated, such as the requirement to wear special armbands or mark your houses, and certain other things which were mentioned in the press during the war did not pan out. This particular text, if you page to the very end, I believe, is dated June of 1993 and has not been amended ever since. Well, this doesn't -- oh, yes, here. The summer of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You've lied once again, that non-Serbs had to wear white armbands. And when you realised that what you stated was not true, why didn't you write a new text? Why didn't you apologise to the intellectual public, saying, "I made a mistake at such-and-such a time. It's not true that there were racist laws or, rather, laws against misogynation;" why didn't you do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, again Mr. Seselj can't just simply accuse the witness of lying. He's done that several times. It's improper, and we object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Seselj, this question about lying or false testimony, a person may in good faith say certain things which are untrue. It doesn't mean that he had the intention to lie or to deceive anybody. This is the difficult point. When you say that, "You are now bearing false testimony and you are saying things which are untrue," first of all, you have to prove it. And even if you have proved it, one has to say that this was done deliberately, willfully, with an intention to deceive, because in good faith one can be mistaken. I could say that I see 25 armchairs in the room, and in fact there were not 25 but only 20, and someone could say that I made a false statement. While in good faith I thought there were 20, there might have been 24, that's the problem. So the Prosecution objects. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Also, Your Honours, I do note on page 76, lines 6 through 9, I didn't want to interrupt Mr. Seselj, but we do also object to him characterizing Biljana Plavsic as a collaborator. That is also inappropriate, and of course the use of the term "collaborator" can be interpreted in a number of different ways. We do object also to that characterization of Mrs. Plavsic. And, again, just one other issue, if I could before the break, Your Honours. I do have the Congressional testimony of Mr. Riedlmayer, which I'm prepared to re-disclose to Mr. Seselj, but I do indicate that the -- we did have Mr. Riedlmayer's testimony to the US Congress translated into Serbian, and that was disclosed to Mr. Seselj on April 2nd, 2008, under disclosure receipt 296. In the event he doesn't have that, I do have an extra copy, both of the receipt and of that transcript here in the courtroom, which I can give him for his possible review and use during the break. So perhaps if the usher could assist me in re-disclosing this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never received this before. This is the first time I have it in my hands. And the fact that you have some kind of a certificate containing a large number of documents, I really cannot check each and every time whether these piles of documents are all there. I mean, I receive them in good faith, but I cannot check each and every document. However, this is not an ordinary citizen. This is not a person who may misspeak, who may make a mistake. This is a Prosecution exhibit. He has a double Master's degree, and when he says that Serbs had laws against the mixing of genes, then he has to have proof for that, because he has scientific aspirations. If he writes all of this without any proof and then he ultimately admits that it's not true, and if he does not then issue a denial himself, then he is a liar. There is no other word to use in connection with that. When I catch someone out this way, a witness, I have the right to say, in cross-examination, that he is a liar. And this is confirmed by case law and jurisprudence, and you know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, when you write that, that there were racial laws, what did you base yourself on to write this? Did you see any evidence? What made it possible for you to write this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was written in 1993, at a time when there was very little information in English available on the conflict in Bosnia and its background. Somebody, a layman, asked me to write a little backgrounder, which I did, and it got posted on the web. This was 15 years ago. At that time, I had not -- the Tribunal didn't exist, the war was still going on, and I had yet to go to Bosnia. Since then, I have learned a great deal, and I would probably be much more circumspect in what I might write. The fact is it was written in an informal circumstance during the war and for a very non-specialised audience. It was not the kind of publication that one formally retracts or amends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but just this is it: If you were aiming at a non-specialised audience, this is all the more the reason to be extremely careful when it comes to your scientific approach. If you're saying things that are more or less true towards experts, they will right away be able to make the difference; but if you're talking to a non-scientific audience, the farmer in Arkansas, you know, who has internet and through the web, since you're an authority in your own country, given your position, this farmer could read, "Oh, this person says there are racial laws," well, and who knows, you know, he would take it at face value. You see my point. This can be very dangerous, you know, when you say things that are only half truths. Do you understand this now, with the hindsight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, sir, but also I would point out that I had to rely, during the war, on information that was publicly available then. What I knew then is not what I'm in a position to know now. And also the difference between something produced informally and something produced for a scientific publication is that in a scientific publication, you are prepared to be reviewed by your peers, you cite sources, and you, you know, cross every "t" and dot every "i". In an informal setting, one is often less careful. The fact is, in 1993, there were published reports making these allegations, there was no way for me to check them. As I pointed out, the Tribunal at that point was not up and functioning yet, and so if my attempt at writing a brief history of which this is only a small segment is in parts flawed, I accept that, but it's something I wrote under different circumstances 15 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's have a 20-minute break. We will resume at 10 after 6.00. We have to stop now because the tapes are almost up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you just tell me how much time I have, please, taking into account the extension of 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Registrar, just before the problem, told me that you had one hour and six minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope, Judges, that you received the two paragraphs from the first instance judgement in the Brdjanin case. I have nothing more to comment, except to state that my name is not mentioned here, nor are any "Seselj's men" or the volunteers of my party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, do you consider me a fascist?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, you have your ideology, of course. Mussolini had his. I've heard people call you a fascist, yes, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, do you think that the Serbian Radical Party, of which I'm still the president, which is the strongest political party in Serbia, that it is a fascist party, in fact? You know that it is the single strongest party in Serbia, it has the largest number of members of Parliament, it is about to form the government, the cabinet. It is very powerful at the local level. So is it a fascist party, in your opinion, as a historian?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, I'm not a political scientist, but I do believe that it espouses extreme nationalism, which some people have characterized as fascist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But I do hope you realise that not all nationalists are fascists. Was de Gaulle a fascist, the greatest French nationalist in the 20th century? There's no doubt about that, is there, but could one say that he was a fascist at all?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: De Gaulle not, maybe, but Le Pen, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you could prove that Le Pen is a fascist?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection. Relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, could you tell us the relevance of all this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I asked the witness whether he considered me to be a fascist. The witness said that he didn't, but that people did say that. I asked him whether the Serbian Radical Party was a fascist party. He said that he couldn't say that it was a fascist party, but that it was a nationalist -- a radical nationalist party, which is not controversial. That is very important for me, because -- could you please show document number 4 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, you published a paper -- or, rather, this is your statement in an article entitled: "Andras Riedlmayer re events in Kosovo." Could you please go to page, I believe -- could you just leaf through it? I think it's page 3, but I'm not sure. In fact, it's page 1. Since I have this version in the Serbian language and this is the English version, you see here that in the middle paragraph, the one that's marked, you stated: "The current political crisis in Serbia -- the beneficiaries of the current political crisis in Serbia are more likely to be the Radicals, who under Seselj's successor, Tomislav Nikolic, have been trying to remake their image into something less scary than the neo-fascist party that they are." So here again you state -- the date of this article is the 13th of March, 2008, so it's just before you came here to testify. You stated that we, the Radicals, are a neo-fascist party; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly wrote this. On the other hand, this is not a publication -- [French interpretation on English channel] It's an e-mail I sent to a friend, who then put it up on his blog. Blogs are web logs. They're informal commentary by people on current events and various other things. It's not a formal publication. I -- as I indicated in my earlier answer to you, there are many people who do, indeed, characterize the SRS as neo-fascist, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This is not about many people. We're talking about you. I'm not interested in what you say about many people. I'm interested in you. And again I caught you lying. You said here that the Serbian Radical Party was a neo-fascist party, and you know that things that are published on web sites, on the internet, are as much published as if they were printed in the newspapers or magazines or if things like that were broadcast on TV, it's published, made public?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection again with, "Again I caught you lying." Even if the witness were expressing an opinion as to the characterization of the SRS, that is not something that in any way, shape, or form could be characterized as a lie. We object to this. And again, Your Honours, we strongly object to the accused calling witnesses liars, false witnesses, et cetera, on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the witness sent an e-mail which was posted on a blog. I'll come back to this later. The interested party is talking about your political party, your successor, and so forth and so on, and then you said, "I caught you lying." "Again I caught you lying." What did he lie about? Could you tell us exactly what you mean by this, because I can't really understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I asked the witness whether he considered me a fascist. He did not say "yes." Then I asked him if he considered the Serbian Radical Party, and I am an active and current president, whether it was a fascist party. He did not say "yes." He said this is something that can be heard from other people, but he did not say that this was his position. And now I found an article where it transpires that he labels the Serbian Radical Party a neo-fascist party. I'm attacking his credibility, and I think I'm very successful in it. I think -- I hope that you already realise that, that I was successful in impeaching this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, at first Mr. Seselj asked you whether you considered him as a fascist. You answered by saying, "I'm not into politics. I don't know." Then he asked further questions, and you said -- in a few words, you said "no." And then we have a document cropping up where it is written, black on white, that the Serbian Radical Party and its members are neo-fascists, but that some are trying to reshape their image, such as Nikolic. You see that there is a difference between what you said earlier and what you have written in this paper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You will note, Your Honour, that I was saying that it has been characterized as such. I didn't say that I didn't think so. But if I have to be rude, I'll say it. The Radical Party, in its programme, historically at the time of the Balkan wars and during the Kosovo war of 1999, had a programme that was in many ways justly characterizable as fascist. It has been trying to remake its image, and that's what I was commenting on. It's simply a comment on the current political situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going to go into this debate, because we have not been seized of the question as to whether this party is this or this party is that. However, I would like to tell you how surprised I am. You have already testified in a number of major cases which were picked up by the media. You knew that you were called here as an expert witness, not just a plain witness but an expert witness for the Prosecution. You know that, by definition, an expert witness is somebody that is totally unbiased, that is not prejudiced against anything, but on March 13, 2008, just a few weeks ago, you send a document which was posted by the recipient on a blog. You're saying this is informal. Very well, but of course you know that the communication -- everything is on the internet, everything is on web sites and on blogs and everyone knows everything. Didn't you consider that by sending this e-mail to a person, when you were supposed to testify just a few weeks later, this could create a problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was rather surprised when he posted it on the blog. I had sent it to him as a private communication. This was not meant for a general public. On the other hand, I am an observer of current events, like anybody else, and make comments about current events, including political events. My understanding is that as an expert here, I'm an expert on matters other than politics, and as such, anything I've said about the matters relating to my expertise before this Tribunal has yet to be challenged, in terms of its veracity or its fairness. I took an oath when I took the witness stand here, and I promised to say the truth, as I saw it, and certainly I've been doing my best to do that. You know, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to add, after what I read in the transcript, that the witness said -- answered negatively to the question put by Mr. Seselj, when he asked him whether the witness thought that Mr. Seselj was a fascist. This is when he said "no." As far as the party is concerned and as far as this paper that was posted on a blog, there, there is no answer, or at least the answer that we have is a bit ambiguous, and the only answer we have is the following. The witness says: "I believe that Seselj's party espouses a very -- an extreme nationalist view, and that some could characterize this party as fascist."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, you went on to say there were some fascist parts in the Serbian Radical Party programme earlier. Could you please be more specific? What elements in the policies and activities of the Serbian Radical Party were actually fascist?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's been a long time since I've read your party's programme, but I do recall reading it in the 1990s, and some of the items in your programme, referring to Kosovo, certainly sounded to me like coming from that point of view, from an extreme point of view. It's been a decade since I saw that, and it's not the matter of my expertise. If I'd known that you were going to ask me about that, I would have reread your programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, it is one thing to be extremist, and it's a completely different thing to be a fascist. It's one thing to be radical, which means to go to the root of the things - that's why our party is called the Radical Party - and it's a completely different thing to be fascist. Have you ever found, in the programme of the Serbian Radical Party, any elements that would indicate that we were opposed to individualism?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection. This goes way beyond -- this goes way beyond the scope of the witness's expertise and his report and his testimony. This issue -- this topic has been questioned on and it's exhausted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are partially right. This witness is also a historian and well read. Witness, please, if you can answer, please answer. If you believe that this goes beyond your field of competence, just say, "I can't answer." You're the best one to know how to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a historian, my training is in Ottoman history, not in current political events. I believe this goes beyond my expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, it suffices that I read Philip Hitti's book. It's a rather lengthy one, 700 pages. It was in Serbian, The History of the Ottoman Empire, and on the basis of that one book, I can -- I now say that I'm an expert in the matter. I can't say that. You had general studies in history, and you know that fascism, Nazism, communism, that they're characterized by collectivist ideology; isn't that right? So in the programme of the Serbian Radical Party, did you find anything resembling a collectivistic ideology? Let's take things in order, so "yes" or "no" to that question.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's beyond my expertise to talk about that. As I told you, it's been over a decade since I saw the programme of your party. By now, most of what I retain of it is a general impression rather than the specifics. I am not in a position to go through it point by point with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, how, then, are you able to state that the Serbian Radical Party is a neo-fascist party? You must have proof and evidence of that and say that, for example, we advocate collectivism, that we're opposed to democracy, that we are anti-intellectualists, that we're racists, and things like that, that we're against a multiparty system, that we're some variation of some social Darwinism. It's easy to put a label and say "fascist," but if you do that, if you label someone, you must have evidence to show that. You just slap this on someone, slap a label on a party, and finish there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, if you are using this argument like you have in the past, to test the credibility of the witness, I understand full well. You have done this, you've tested his credibility, and we'll see. But if you wish to address the merits of these questions, you must understand that he is not here to talk about those questions. He is not competent in that area. His report deals with different subjects. So if you go beyond the question of the credibility of this witness, then of course we need to address the relevance of this. And to my mind, your last questions were not relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Lattanzi, the total time of those two minutes that you deducted from my time because of abusing the objections during the examination-in-chief, I challenged the professionalism of this witness and his expert report, and I am challenging and destroying his credibility. And once I complete this process, there will be nothing left of this witness's credibility, so that's my aim. Why should I speak of professionalism when he's not professional in anything, an expert in anything. If we talk about photography and the lack of a flash, not enough light when photographs were taken, or to talk about what some man might have told him in a location, I don't think those are professional questions. So the two minutes that you took away from me, I managed to destroy him, in professional terms, and now I'm turning to his moral credibility. I'm challenging that, and I have a new question for you, Mr. Riedlmayer, since I still have not destroyed your credibility as much as I would like to have done, although the results are catastrophic thus far.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But in testifying in the Milosevic trial and the Krajisnik trial, you also testified about the burning of the largest library in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the building of the municipal building in Sarajevo, in fact; do you remember that? The town hall?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You wrote an extensive article on the subject, "From the ashes of the cultural heritage of Bosnia-Herzegovina," words to that effect, and you describe the town hall which was set alight, and said that 1.500.000 books were burned in the process; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And that is your article dating to 2002; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the Prosecutor gave me a report by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, dated the 20th of September, 1993, and that is a document IT-03-67-57/12 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Those numbers were far too fast for the interpreter to repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It was a document published nine years before you published your article, and in paragraph 25 of that document -- I hope you have the document on your screens, on e-court already. I have adapted myself, you see, to e-court, and I hope the Prosecution has done the same. Anyway, in paragraph 25, this is what it says: According to the report by the Fund for Assistance to the National and University Library in Sarajevo, the fire caused by Serb bombing on the 23rd and 24th of August, 1992, destroyed the depot on the upper level, and the lending out inventory, that is to say, the library cards and everything else, all the records, all manuals, and the musical documents, music documents, what was retained was the Incanabula, which are important medieval manuscripts, as you know as a historian, other manuscripts, archives, rare books, the Bosnian collection, and a large portion of the collection of the periodicals of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not to mention some titles from other libraries that were stored in that building. In other words, the damage was luckily less than was at first feared, when it came to the loss of irreplaceable documents, but it remains very serious. Perhaps 600.000 books or titles are concerned. Dr. Mustafic, 1.500.000 library units. So nine years before your article appeared, the Council of Europe made these observations, that is to say, that the most valuable works were saved in the National Library of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they remain intact, although a large number of books were destroyed, but they were more recent editions that can be replenished. It is easier for me to learn of somebody beating someone than when a book is burnt. Anyway, I spent a lot of time working in that library, and there I differ from you, because the library was very useful to me in my life and work. Anyway, you have an official report here, and you continue to say "1.500.000 books." You quote that figure. Now, there are some exotic things here that appear. For instance, you say that while the fire was being put out, the Serbs, from their surrounding hills, used machine fire to cut the fire hoses. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Riedlmayer, that there are no hills where Serb positions were located from which any machine-gun can fire into the town hall building; that's quite impossible?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Several things on that, since it was a complex question. First of all, that report was from 1993, six months after the destruction of the National University Library. At that point, Sarajevo was still under siege. The rescued volumes were in storage in several locations. Full assessment had yet to be made. After the war, more extensive assessments were made and published, and I refer to them in my expert report to the -- for the Milosevic trial. Secondly, yes, some special collections that were in the basement of the library were saved largely because of a lack of oxygen. The intensity of the fire was such that it drew all the oxygen upward, and the items in the basement, to which some of the more valuable items in the collection had been moved, survived. But the volume of material that was saved is relatively small. I was shown six or seven large trunks that contained some of the most precious items in the collection. However, a very large part, a majority of -- for example, the Bosnian periodicals collection was lost. This is material that no library, other than the National Library, collected to such an extent. A large percentage of the deposit publications, a fairly complete collection of everything that had been printed in Bosnia from the mid-19th century until the war, a large percentage of that vanished. What remained has been estimated at roughly 100.000 items. What was lost included not only books, but special collections, maps, photographs, and other items. So the 1.500.000 is a very firm estimate of the number of library items that was lost, this according to Bosnian colleagues who had published extensive material about it. As to what happened to the firemen, I interviewed a number of firemen who had been in the fire brigade at the time of the attack on the National Library. What they reported was that the water had been cut at the time of the attack and that they had to expose themselves by running hoses to the Neretva River, to pump water from there. When you are out on the "obala", on the promenade along the river, you are in plain sight from several directions, from the mountaintops, which were indeed held by Serb forces. The fire hoses were then snaked into the narrow street between Bascarsija and the library. I have raw video footage of the firemen trying to put out the fire, with the fire hoses spurting water everywhere because they had been punctured in numerous places. What the calibre of ammunition was used to achieve this effect is beyond my expertise, because I'm not a military expert, but I was told by the firemen that,(a), they were fired on with heavy calibre and that anti-aircraft munitions, aimed at street level, were shot at --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, that's a very long story. Tell me, how long did those firemen need to rush to the Neretva River and take up some water from there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hoses were run from the library, across the main street, and into the river. I didn't ask them how long that took, but presumably if hoses are leaking all over the place, one placement may not have been enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, for them to run to the Neretva River, they --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: -- they would need 15 days. This man Mustafic, Dr. Mustafic, says that 600.000 titles were burnt, and later on it turned out that less were burnt. But you should know that for days before the fire broke out, the Muslim authorities used trucks to pull out the most valuable books from the town hall, which means that the fire was prepared. Do you know that during that fire itself, in Sarajevo there was the most prominent French Serb-hater present, Henry Bernard Levy, or the other way around, but "Levy," anyway. Have you heard of him and that he was there at the time? Have you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard of him. I have not read anything he's written --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Without any moral scruples, that man is, so you don't have to read about him or hear about him. He has no scruples and he is anti-Serb, he hates the Serbs. And he bragged that the famous Sarajevo "hagada," that is to say, a manuscript that the Jews brought when they were persecuted from Spain, that he personally saved this manuscript. Did the firemen tell you about that there, the ones that you interviewed?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if he bragged about it, then he was not telling the truth. First of all, the Sarajevo "hagada" was never in the National Library, it was in the Zemaljski Muzej, the National Museum. And, secondly, I doubt that he personally had anything to do with its rescue. It was evacuated from the museum weeks before the National Library was shelled. What I rely on is not statements like that, but video footage of what happened, statements from eyewitnesses, professional assessments published in the journals of the local librarians' association, interviews with librarian colleagues. You can read about it in my expert report. Obviously, it has more detail than the article you just cited, but, nevertheless, I would disagree with those preliminary figures from 1993. As for the question that -- alleging that the books were evacuated before the attack, that presupposes,(a), that they either knew of the attack or that the attack didn't happen and it was somehow ignited from within. I have spoken to enough eyewitnesses who have seen the shells landing, independent multiple sources, that I have no doubt that the library was, indeed, shelled, and it was shelled with incendiary munitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Your sources are unidentified, Mr. Riedlmayer, and on the videotape that you mention, there was no explosion of a shell, nor a machine-gun firing? Just say "yes" or "no". That wasn't on the tape, was it? To use the time I have, I'd like to show you another document, so don't take up my time. If you're able to say "yes" or "no", if not --

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... very short. I will simply say that the videotape footage was taken the day after the attack. The attack occurred at nightfall on one day and the fire was still burning the next day, and so it doesn't show the original shelling because it was getting dark when the original shelling happened. But I talked to people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You've answered the question, yes, and that's an extensive answer and I'm quite satisfied. Now, Madam Usher, document number 2 on the overhead projector, please. Have you heard of the Centre for Research into Crimes against the Serb People, the leader of which is Mr. Milivoj Ivanisevic? Have you heard of the centre?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have a document which I received from Mr. Ivanisevic, himself, and I would like to show you parts of that document; not the entire document, very brief excerpts. Anyway, he describes his knowledge, what he knows about the burning of the town hall in Sarajevo and says the following: "During my work in compiling studies on the Serb victims of Sarajevo, I would like to remind you that there were an enormous number of Serb victims who, according to present knowledge, amounts to 5.776 victims and 859 persons of Serb ethnicity whose fate is still unknown. And I came across material which relates to self-shelling, as well as documents and material which relate to the destruction of cultural monuments and the cultural heritage in this town. One of those cases, in my opinion, deserves special attention. That is the burning of the town hall in which the National and University Library was located. This event, although it was early in the morning, at around 3.00 or 4.00 a.m., was directly broadcast live by all television stations, CNN Sarajevo and others, just as happened in all other cases when the Muslims in Sarajevo organised spectacles of this kind. In the surrounding streets, Vasko Miskin [phoen], Veselin Maslesa, Veliki and Mali Curciluk and others, around the Evropa Hotel, you could hear people talking loudly. There was a lot of noise, soldiers wearing black uniforms shouting to one another from the unit under Commander Cele [as interpreted]. They were boasting amongst themselves how, that with a Frenchman, they set fire to the town hall, and they stressed the capabilities and skill of their French collaborators, especially, and all the inhabitants in the streets could hear this. "Remembrance of this event was published in a programme, 'Klica [phoen] Kulture' on TV Sarajevo, a sort of roundtable held on the premises of the town hall that was burnt down on the 6th of December, 2001, in a programme led by some foreigner, but several guests took part. Among them was Mr. Henry Bernard Levy, Mrs. Cupicic, a guest from Belgrade. Mr. Henry Bernard Levy joined that programme, was triumphant in showing the Sarajevo 'hagada,' which allegedly he himself saved from the fire. And he testified to the fact that at the time when the town hall was set on fire, he happened to be present, and as he said, he saved the 'hagada'. "I would like to remind you that many books from the library were taken out several days earlier, but that books remained in the library which were mostly by Serb authors. We don't believe that the 'hagada' was among them. After so many years, this is the first public testimony about the presence of Mr. Levy during that tragical event as far as our culture is concerned. They didn't know the name of the Frenchman present and it was only the competence of Commander Cele who spoke of this Frenchman." What do you think of that, Mr. Riedlmayer, as a historian and as an expert witness for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that, first of all, I'm not prepared to take this without some supporting evidence of some sort. It's somebody's assertion. During the war, there were numerous different rationales given for the shelling of the library. It was variously claimed that it had been used as a military position - this is what Mr. Milosevic subsequently claimed. Mr. Karadzic, in September of the same year, 1992, when the library was burned, told Elivisal [phoen] that the Muslims had set it on fire because they didn't like its architecture. There were all kinds of allegations and rumours, but I simply have trouble believing anything that's stated in this. I've never heard Bernard Henry-Levy claiming that he had rescued a book from the burning library that was not in the burning library. I don't exclude the possibility that he may have done so, but if he did, he is boasting, because the "hagada" was never stored in the National Library. So I don't think much of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, is it clear to you that the treasury of the National Library is equally important to Serbs, Muslims and Croats who live in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that there is no way in which it can be more valuable to the Muslims there than to the local Serbs? Is that not fully clear to you?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. The National Library was the repository of the cultural heritage of everyone in Bosnia. The only reason I can see why it would have been shelled is, (a), it was a Bosnian national institution and Bosnian national identity, and Bosnian national institutions were abhorred by the ideology of the Bosnian Serb forces like Mr. Karadzic and his SDS. And, secondly, you can see --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Riedlmayer, there is no national identity of Bosnia, Bosnian national identity. There is only the multinational identity of Bosnia. There is no Bosnian nation. Serbs, Croats and Muslims lived in Bosnia, and all the way up to the Second World War, the Orthodox Serbs were the most numerous group. There is no Bosnian national identity. This started only during the course of the war, when somebody proclaimed the Bosnian Muslims to be Bosniaks, so that they could seize Bosnian cultural heritage. Why would Serbs be less Bosniak than Muslims? If I was born in Sarajevo, if both of my parents are from Herzegovina, am I not a Bosniak, in terms of my territorial and national belonging? Why would a Muslim be more of a Bosniak than I am as a Serb Orthodox if my folk lived there since time immemorial?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
